a.summary: The only non-method-scoped suppression added by this commit is a class-level `@SuppressWarnings("removal")` over all 603 lines of the file whose own doc comment declares it the compiler-enforced pin for the published interface shape; it needs to cover just 7 sites living in exactly 2 methods.
a.failure_scenario: A future release marks another abstract `Transaction` member `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)` — say `sign(int, Signer)`. `PreV1Transaction` (line 47) implements every pre-v1 abstract method by delegation, so it would implement the newly removal-scheduled one silently: the file-wide suppression means javac emits neither the per-site `[removal]` warning nor the file-level "uses or overrides a deprecated API that is marked for removal" note anywhere in the compile. The file's stated purpose — "the published-library rule enforced by the compiler instead of by review" (line 43-45) — is exactly what stops working for removal-class changes.

b.summary: This fixture — the repo's compiler-enforced sentinel for the published pre-v1 `Transaction` surface — got a class-scope `@SuppressWarnings("removal")` while the other eight sites in the same commit got method-scope ones, so it will absorb every future removal warning silently.
b.failure_scenario: MIGRATION.md:5-8 says the legacy/v0 transaction factories' deprecation is deferred until v1 activates on mainnet. When that deprecation lands as `@Deprecated(forRemoval = true)`, the two nested implementations here (which declare the complete 25.10.0 abstract surface at lines 71 and 404, plus overrides at 435, 456 and 464) emit zero `[removal]` warnings. The one file in the repo that exists to show the blast radius on external implementors shows nothing, and the next reviewer has to re-derive the impact by hand.

instructions.question: How does the defect described by `b` relate to the defect described by `a`?
instructions.focus: Compare the defects, not the wording. Two findings about the same code can still be different defects.

criteria: Different defects: fixing the defect `a` describes would leave the defect `b` describes unfixed, even when both sit in the same code.
The same underlying defect, but `b` narrows it, re-scopes which instances or inputs it covers, or reports it at a different place. Not a different defect in adjacent code.
The same defect restated in different words: fixing one fixes the other.

claims_new_evidence.instructions: Does `b` cite evidence that `a` does not?

criteria.true: `b` names a file, test, command, observation, or reproduction that `a` does not mention.
criteria.false: `b` cites nothing beyond what `a` already cites, or cites nothing at all.
